chunks: "Sensors show up anywhere a system needs to know about the world, so I group the applications by what the system does with the measurement.

First, control: a motor driver measures current and rotor position to run a field-oriented loop, a thermostat measures temperature to switch a heater, a drone uses a gyroscope and accelerometer to stay level.

Second, protection and safety: a battery management system watches cell voltage, current and temperature and disconnects the pack when something goes out of range; a car's airbag controller watches an accelerometer for a crash.
Third, user experience: your phone's ambient light sensor sets screen brightness, the proximity sensor turns the screen off at your ear, and the accelerometer rotates the display and counts steps.

Fourth, monitoring and diagnostics: vibration sensors on a machine predict bearing failure, environmental sensors log temperature and humidity, and medical wearables use optical sensors for heart rate.
For each one, the interesting engineering is the requirement. A thermostat needs 0.

5 degrees Celsius and one reading per second, an airbag accelerometer needs tens of g range and a deploy decision within a few tens of milliseconds, and a wearable needs microamps because it sleeps most of the time."
